newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Bildt to make welcome return to Swedish politics.
newsitem.headline: Bildt to make welcome return to Swedish politics.

text.p: Carl Bildt, widely praised for his work as the major powers' mediator in Bosnia, is preparing to return to Swedish politics.
Many Swedes are relieved. They say his absence left a gap and conservatives need his leadership to prepare for next year's election challenge to the ruling Social Democrats.

Bildt, a former prime minister, is the leader of Sweden's opposition conservative party, the Moderates. He took on the Bosnian mission after losing the September 1994 election to the left-of-centre Social Democrats.
And he has been earning kudos in the Balkans, the popularity for the Social Democrats has begun to wane.
He is now expected to shift the Moderates into a higher gear to prepare for the next election in September 1998, push a firm pro-Europe line, and enliven Sweden's tired, political debate.
"There really has been no clear opposition leader in Bildt's absence and no one in parliament to rally the non-Socialist parties," Stockholm University's professor of politics, Olaf Ruin, said.
"He's not just needed by the opposition but the government also needs a concrete person to argue with and attack."

A spokeswoman for Bildt said he preferred not to comment about the possible date of his return to Sweden for fear of jeopardising his effectiveness in his last months in Bosnia but he would be back this year.
Most political commentators expected Bildt to return by the summer in time for the start of the parliamentary year in mid-September, giving him a year to prepare for the election.

But few held out much hope of Bildt, despite his popularity, being able to beat the Social Democrats at the next election, even though the latest opinion polls have levelled the parties, the two biggest of seven in Swedish parliament.
For the first time since 1991 support for the Social Democrats led by Prime Minister Goran Persson has fallen below 30 percent and the Moderates are only 0.5 percent behind.

But analysts said it was the Left Party and Green Party that were capaturing supporters from the Social Democrats, not the bourgeois parties like the Moderates, Centre Party, Liberals and Christian Democrats.
"I think Bildt is coming back to try to win the 1998 election," Anders Sannerstedt, professor of politics at Lund University, told Reuters.

"But he'll be keeping his options open. If he does not win the election -- and I think the Social Democrats will form a minority government again -- I wouldn't be surprised if he left the chairmanship of the Moderates for an international career."
The ever-serious Bildt, 47, will return to Sweden on a high, the most successful Swedish politician on the world stage since former prime minister Olaf Palme who was killed in 1986.
"Bildt is looked upon as a bit of a Swedish hero. No one else has the same international prestige as him," said Ruin.
"But that can change a lot within six months of coming back because he'll be involved in unpleasant domestic affairs."
Terry Carlbom, politics professor at Uppsala University, said Bildt's return would revitalise political debates, particularly on issues like nuclear power and European currency union.
"A strong opposition would never have let the government be as lacking as the Social Democrats, soft peddling European issues, and Bildt will right this," Carlbom said.

Although his prospects on the home front are uncertain, the lanky, bespectacled Bildt is seen as Sweden's main hope to shine in the international arena, with his life dedicated to politics and with clear, international ambitions.
After leaving university without graduating, he entered parliament in 1979. In 1986, aged 37, he was chosen as chairman of the Moderates, becoming Sweden's youngest political leader.
Five years later, in October 1991, a parliamentary vote of no confidence brought down the Social Democrat government and Bildt became Sweden's first conservative premier for 61 years.
"He started off with a baby face image but that has been replaced by a far more worldly image," Carlbom said.
